questions.question: Which feature of the Indian Constitution reflects the idea that the powers of government are divided among the executive, legislative, and judicial branches to prevent the concentration of power?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Separation of powers**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• ** Executive**

 
 
• Article 53 of the Constitution of India states that the executive power of the Union shall be vested in the President. 
 
• However, the President exercises this power on the advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister. 
 
• This is known as the "advice and consent" system.
 
• The President has the power to appoint the Prime Minister, dissolve the Lok Sabha, and make certain key appointments. 
 
• However, he can only do these things on the advice of the Council of Ministers. 
 
• The President is also the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces.
 
• In practice, the real executive power in India lies with the Council of Ministers. 
 
• The Prime Minister is the head of the Council of Ministers and is responsible for the day-to-day running of the government. 
 
• The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
 
• The Parliament is the supreme law-making body in India. 
 
• It has the power to make laws, amend the Constitution, and remove the President from office. 
 
• However, the Parliament cannot interfere with the executive powers of the President.
 
• So, while the executive power of the Union vests in the President, it is actually exercised by the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister. 
 
• This is a reflection of the parliamentary system of government that is practised in India.
 
 
 
• **​ Legislative**
 
 
• The legislature is prohibited from acting in an executive or judicial capacity by the doctrine of separation of powers.
 
• Legislative and judicial authority are not subject to executive control.
 
• and the judicial branch is not permitted to use the other two powers.
 
• As with the British Parliament, the Indian Parliament is therefore able to pass legislation that both quantitatively and qualitatively delegated legislative power.
 
• In the absence of any constitutional restrictions, any amount of legislative power could be delegated as long as the delegating body maintained its own legislative authority.
 
 
 
• **Judicial **
 
 
• The power of judicial review relates to the Review of the organization of the judiciary.
 
• It is the power exerted by the courts of a country to examine the actions of the legislatures, and executive and administrative arms of government and to ensure that such actions conform to the provisions of the nation’s Constitution.
 
• The judicial review implies the power to ensure that laws passed by the legislature are in compliance with the provisions of the Constitution.
 
• Judicial review is considered a basic structure of the constitution (Indira Gandhi vs Raj Narain Case 1975).

questions.question: In the context of a government budget, what does the term "fiscal deficit" represent?

options.text: The surplus funds available for public spending
The difference between government revenue and government expenditure
The portion of the budget allocated for defense spending

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The difference between government revenue and government expenditure**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Fiscal Deficit__

 
 
• A fiscal deficit is a shortfall in a government's income compared with its spending. The government that has a fiscal deficit is spending beyond its means.
 
• A fiscal deficit is calculated as a percentage of gross domestic product (GDP), or simply as total dollars spent in excess of income.
 
• A fiscal deficit is different from fiscal debt. The latter is the total debt accumulated over years of deficit spending.
 
• A government creates a fiscal deficit by spending more money than it takes in from taxes and other revenues excluding debt.
 
• The gap between income and spending is closed by government borrowing.
 
• The fiscal deficit calculations are based on two components — income and expenditure.
 
• The U.S. government has had a fiscal deficit in most of the years since World War II.

questions.question: Economists call unemployment prevailing in Indian farms as __________ unemployment.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**disguised**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• Unemployment occurs when a person who is actively searching for employment is unable to find work.
 
• It is often used as a measure of the health of the economy. 
 
• Types of Unemployment
 
• Disguised Unemployment:
 
 
• The phenomenon when more people are employed than actually needed. Hence statement 1 is correct.
 
• Example: agricultural and the unorganized sectors of India.
 
 
 
• Seasonal Unemployment:
 
 
• Unemployment occurs during certain seasons of the year.
 
• Example: Agricultural laborers.
 
 
 
• Structural Unemployment:
 
 
• Unemployment arising from the mismatch between the jobs and the skills of the available workers in the market. Hence statement 2 is correct.
 
• Many people do not get jobs due to a lack of requisite skills and due to the poor educational level.
 
 
 
• Cyclical Unemployment:
 
 
• It is the result of the business cycle. Hence statement 3 is not correct.
 
• Unemployment rises during recessions and declines with economic growth. 
 
 
 
• ​Technological Unemployment:
 
 
• It is the loss of jobs due to changes in technology.
 
 
 
• ​Frictional Unemployment:
 
 
• Frictional Unemployment is also known as Search Unemployment. Hence statement 4 is not correct.
 
• It refers to the time lag between the jobs when an individual is searching for a new job or is switching between the jobs.
 
 
 
• ​Vulnerable Employment:
 
 
• This means people are working informally without proper job contracts.
 
• These persons are deemed ‘unemployed’ since records of their work are never maintained.

questions.question: HYVS in case of green revolution, stands for:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**High Yielding Variety Seeds**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The green revolution is the rise in agricultural productivity, particularly in developing nations, made possible by the use of novel crops and farming techniques.
 
• Given that he started the Green Revolution in India, M. S. Swaminathan is regarded as its father. He was motivated by Norman Borlaug's effort.
 
• Norman Borlaug started the Green Revolution movement in the 1960s. He is referred to as the "Father of the Green Revolution" globally. For his efforts in creating High Yielding Varieties (HYVs) of wheat, it resulted in him being awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970. 
 
• In order to enhance food production and reduce hunger and poverty, high-yielding cultivars of rice and wheat were first introduced in India in the 1960s.
 
• In Punjab, the Green Revolution in India was first implemented in late 1966 or early 1967 as a part of a development initiative launched by international donor organisations and the Indian government.
 
• One of the innovative techniques created during the Green Revolution was drip irrigation. This technology allowed water to drop slowly and steadily to the roots of plants, saving water and promoting more sustainable agriculture.
 
• India has achieved significant progress thanks to the Green Revolution, which has brought about a previously unheard-of level of food security. It has helped many non-poor people avoid the poverty and hunger they would have otherwise faced while lifting a significant number of poor people out of poverty

questions.question: The partition of Bengal took place in ____________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1905**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The idea of partition of Bengal was brought up during the tenure of Lord Curzon for administrative reasons.
 
• Partition of Bengal took place on October 16, 1905.
 
• The reason cited by the British government was that the smaller states can be better administered.
 
• But the actual reason was to shatter the Hindu-Muslim unity.
 
• Bengal was to divide into the following:
 
 
• Eastern Bengal: Eastern part of Bengal and including Assam in it with its capital at Dacca.
 
• Western province: It included the western Bengal, Odisha and Bihar with its capital at Calcutta (Kolkata now).
 
 
 
• The province was to be divided on the following bases:
 
 
• Language: Separating Hindi speaking regions from Bengali speaking regions.
 
• Religion: Western Bengal included Hindu majority areas while the other one had Muslim majority areas.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

Anti partition Movement:

 
• Opposing the decision of dividing the state, people came out on the streets of Bengal in protest.
 
• People showcased the Hindu-Muslim unity in various processions.
 
• The day of partition was observed as 'National Day of Mourning'.
 
• People came out on streets singing 'Bande Mataram' and 'Amar Sonar Bangla'.
 
• On the day of Raksha Bandhan Hindus and the Muslims tied rakhis on the wrists of each other as a symbol of Brotherhood.

• The Buddha was born into an aristocratic family in the Shakya clan but eventually renounced lay life.
 
• According to Buddhist tradition, after several years of mendicancy, meditation, and asceticism, he awakened to understand the mechanism which keeps people trapped in the cycle of rebirth.
 
• The Buddha then traveled throughout the Ganges plain teaching and building a religious community.
 
• He taught a middle way between sensual indulgence and the severe asceticism found in the Indian sramaṇa movement.
 
• He taught a training of the mind that included ethical training, self-restraint, and meditative practices such as jhana and mindfulness.
 
• The Buddha also critiqued the practices of Brahmin priests, such as animal sacrifice and the caste system.
